title: Bidirectional A* Finds Routes in Reykjavík Fast!
description: Watch Bidirectional A* expand two search frontiers—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet. This visualization uses real-world street-map graph ideas to show how heuristic guidance reduces explored paths dramatically.
ig_caption:
🌍🧠 Reykjavík street maps meet Bidirectional A*!

In this visualization, the route isn’t found by searching outward from just one point—Bidirectional A* runs two coordinated A* searches at once: 🚀 forward from the start and 🔙 backward from the destination. Each side expands nodes using a heuristic (think: “estimated distance to the meeting frontier”), and the moment the two waves touch, the algorithm reconstructs the shortest path across the combined graph.

📍Graph theory connection: treat the street network as a weighted graph where intersections are nodes and road segments are edges (with costs like distance/time). On real map data, this approach can significantly cut the search space because it limits how far each frontier needs to grow before a guaranteed-optimal solution emerges (when heuristics are consistent/admissible in the typical A* sense).

⚙️ Swipe into the math vibe: nodes + edges → priority queues → heuristic-driven expansions → frontier meeting → path recovery ✅

👉 Want a version with different heuristics (e.g., straight-line distance vs. travel-time cost)? Comment your choice and I’ll generate the next reel!

yt_description:
Bidirectional A* Pathfinding Visualization in Reykjavík! 🌍

In this YouTube Shorts, we model real street maps as a weighted graph and run Bidirectional A* (two simultaneous A* searches from start and goal) to meet in the middle for faster route discovery. Watch how heuristics guide node expansions, how the frontier meeting reconstructs the shortest path, and why bidirectional search can reduce explored states.

#pathfinding #algorithms #computerscience
